chapter: Later career, civil service and jazz seminars
title: Music Dial column and Philadelphia union board
summary: In Philadelphia he wrote for Music Dial, served two years on the executive board of Local 274, and stays active with his day job and lodge.

story.theme_name: The musicians' union: cards, locals, and the Black-white merger
story.community_name: The musicians' union: cards, scale and the black-white merger

blocks.x: Well, one thing, you know, we never mentioned, but during that time you were in Philadelphia, you became a journalist and wrote a column in a New York magazine called Music Dial.
That's true.
How long did you do that?

Well, I did that -- that happened in '43 to '44, and I came back here, moved back to New York in about November of '44. Then I stayed because I was going over, commuting for being the dean on the executive board of Local #274, elected.
Oh, in Philly?
In Philly, yeah. Yeah, I was elected executive board member.
Well, how long were you on that?
Two years.
Yeah?
Uh-huh.
Have you ever done anything with this union in New York?
No, and I could have been appointed as a delegate, but I wouldn't take it now because since (Unintelligible) -- Jack Wilson died here about a month and a half ago. I wasn't going to bother with it.
No. Well, you know, that's —
(Simultaneous remarks)
-- about 13 or 20 years ago it was a little bit different, but I was doing so much gig work, playing for different clubs and fraternity -- for the fraternity and then working on my day job too, so --
Yeah. What was your day job?
I work for City College.
Oh, the City College job, yeah. Yeah. Yeah, well, I mean you've done -- really kept very active then.
Yeah, very active. See, between that and the lodge too, so --
Yeah. Well, I mean (unintelligible) it's very important too, isn't it?
Yeah, very nice.
You know, all the nights you were -- I mean if you just sat at home.
Oh, no.
You -- that's not good, is it?
No good.
